pairs.locus: Poggio, Facetiae 19 (Exhortatio Cardinalis ad armigeros Pontificis)
pairs.question: Cur tu non et ad hoc prandium una nobiscum accedis?
pairs.answer: Tempus prandii nondum est mihi, quoniam nondum esurio.
pairs.derivation: Setup: the Cardinal had urged soldiers that the fallen would dine with God and the angels, then withdrew from battle. A soldier asks why the Cardinal does not come along to that lunch. Dropped the speech tags 'inquit' and 'At ille' from question and answer. The answer is a single complete sentence; nothing follows it (the facetia ends). No interior trimming needed.

pairs.question: Te igitur culpas?
pairs.derivation: The Patriarch, after Biracus' witty self-criticism ('si bonum caput haberem...'), asks 'Te igitur culpas?'. Biracus answers that he blames not himself but his head. Dropped speech tags 'ait Patriarcha', 'Tum ille', 'inquit'. Self-contained: the question and answer turn on the 'caput' wordplay already present in both. Answer is the complete reply; the authorial closing comment follows the cut.

pairs.question: Curnam ergo, si nihil habes, ploras?
pairs.derivation: Minacius, having gambled everything away, weeps; asked 'Quidnam est tibi?' he says 'Nihil', prompting the friend to ask why he weeps if he has nothing. The 'si nihil habes' clause makes the question self-contained. Dropped speech tag 'inquit' from the answer. Chose this exchange over the later near-duplicate ('Quare ergo si nihil habes, ploras?' / 'Ob hanc ipsam causam...'); the authorial gloss follows the cut.

pairs.locus: Poggio, Facetiae 57 (Responsio elegans Dantis, poetae Florentini)
pairs.question: Quid est quod tu, cum habearis sapiens ac doctissimus, tamen pauper es et egenus, ego autem stultus et ignarus divitiis praesto?
pairs.answer: Quando ego reperiam dominum mei similem et meis moribus conformem, sicuti tu tuis, et ipse similiter me ditabat.
pairs.derivation: The court fool asks Dante why, though reputed wise and learned, he is poor while the fool is rich. Dante answers that when he finds a lord like himself in character (as the fool has), that lord will likewise enrich him. Dropped speech tags 'inquit ille', 'Tum Dantes', 'inquit'. Answer is Dante's complete reply; the authorial exclamation 'Gravis sapiensque responsio!' follows the cut.

pairs.question: Tu quidnam aspicis?
pairs.answer: Duos magno cursu, ore patulo adventantes canes.
pairs.derivation: In the fox-and-cock fable, the cock has just stretched its neck and risen on its feet as if peering into the distance; the fox asks what it sees, and the cock answers 'two dogs approaching at full speed with open mouths.' Dropped narration 'Vulpes cum dixisset' and tag 'inquit'. A genuine interrogative genuinely answered. Stopped at the end of the cock's reply; the fox's frightened farewell follows the cut. Did not extract the later 'Quonam fugis, aut quid times?' exchange (its reply is more deflection than direct answer).

pairs.locus: Poggio, Facetiae 118 (Responsio Confessoris ad Bernabovem Principem de muliere facta)
pairs.question: Quid ageres, si tu quoque cum ejusmodi muliere in lecto esses?
pairs.answer: Quid me deceret scio, quid vero facturus essem, nescio.
pairs.derivation: Caught dallying with a woman, Bernabò asks his confessor what he would do if he too were in bed with such a woman. The confessor answers that he knows what would be fitting but not what he would actually do. Dropped speech tags 'inquit', 'At ille', 'ait'. Answer is the complete reply; the authorial note that this bent the prince's anger follows the cut.
